premises.text: High-school STEM students lack a way to showcase projects to colleges and employers beyond limited Facebook/team sites
premises.evidence_span: Students are still having trouble exposing their projects, collaborating with one another, and organizing those projects, but not anymore

premises.text: GradFly is a visual portfolio platform where students upload multimedia project stories searchable by topic and category
premises.evidence_span: Introducing GradFly, a portfolio platform for the nation's most innovative minds

premises.text: An algorithm matches students to colleges based on project interests, with school pages including program info and social feeds
premises.evidence_span: We've created an algorithm that pairs the student to a particular college

premises.text: Commendations and skill badges create prestige and a viral incentive for students to keep uploading projects
premises.evidence_span: The more a student has commendations, the more weight and prestige that portfolio has

value.text: STEM students leverage groundbreaking projects to reach colleges, internships, and high-tech employers
value.evidence_span: how do you leverage these projects that students are working on to get into schools like MIT, RPI, Caltech, Cooper Union

causal_links.evidence_span: I witnessed students building some of the most amazing and incredible things I've ever seen. And no one knows about them
GradFly is a visual LinkedIn for high school science, technology, engineering, and math students showcasing their most groundbreaking projects
we would pair her with robust college programs out there that are geared towards robotics
what's gonna keep students excited about uploading projects?

notes: Expose/collaborate/organize pains folded as one student showcase problem (§4.1.6). Upload UI multimedia cascade folded into portfolio platform premise. College-match and badges/commendations split as separately revisable modules with own paths to admissions/engagement value. Embedded student-interview video treated as problem evidence. Ed-tech market size framing excluded. Waitlist/apps-under-development treated as launch status, not premises. Four-domain partition; not a need/product/money triad.
